opus-5.5.text:
Well, thanks for having me, Pieter. I've always been a big reader of history, and I think it gives you a certain humility and a sense of time scales that's useful in a field like ours, which tends to be very caught up in the present moment.

When you read history, you see that ideas have long arcs. Things that seem revolutionary today often have roots going back decades, sometimes centuries. In AI, people sometimes act as if the field started in 2012 with AlexNet. But neural networks go back to the 1940s and 50s, to McCulloch and Pitts, to Rosenblatt's perceptron. Backpropagation was worked out in the 70s and 80s. Convolutional networks owe a lot to Fukushima's neocognitron, and that in turn was inspired by Hubel and Wiesel's work on the visual cortex in the 1960s. So knowing that history helps you see that progress is cumulative, and that ideas which were "failures" in one era can turn out to be right once the computation and the data catch up.

The second thing history teaches is to be skeptical of hype cycles. We've had AI summers and AI winters before. In the 60s people predicted that vision would be solved as a summer project. In the 80s there was enormous excitement about expert systems. Each time, there was real progress, but also overpromising. So when I see claims today that some problem is about to be completely solved, I try to keep a balanced view: yes, the progress is genuinely remarkable, but let's be careful about extrapolating too confidently.

And third, and this is maybe more personal, reading broadly, about the history of science, about evolution, about how human civilization developed, gives me perspective on intelligence itself. If you think about evolution, perception and motor control took hundreds of millions of years to develop. Language and abstract reasoning are very recent additions, maybe a few hundred thousand years. That makes me think the "easy" things for humans, seeing, moving, manipulating objects, are actually the deep, hard problems, and that's partly why I've spent my career on vision and now increasingly on robotics and embodied intelligence. History, in the broadest sense, keeps reminding me what the foundations are.

r001.rationale: It compares past AI summers and winters with present claims, using past cycles to inform a balanced view of current hype.

r002.rationale: It notes that older ideas became useful when computation and data caught up, but does not say the early immaturity of established sciences supports persisting with AI research before results arrive.

r003.rationale: It describes past overpromising and cautions against claims that problems are about to be completely solved, conveying overconfidence about near-term progress.

r004.rationale: It says progress can be cumulative and that computation or data can make older ideas useful, but does not attribute underestimation of long-term AI progress to currently unforeseeable discoveries.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I've always been a bit of a history buff, and I think it gives you a sense of perspective that's very hard to get otherwise when you're in the middle of a field moving as fast as ours.

The first thing history teaches you is humility about timelines. Every generation of AI researchers has believed they were a few years away from solving intelligence. Herbert Simon said it in the fifties, Marvin Minsky said it in the sixties. And they were brilliant people who were simply wrong about how long things would take. So when I hear confident predictions today, I don't dismiss them, but I hold them a little more loosely.

The second thing is that progress in science rarely comes from the direction people expect. If you look at the history of computer vision, the field spent decades on carefully engineered geometric models, and then the breakthrough came from statistics and learning, which many people had considered a side show. The lesson I draw is to keep some breadth, to not become so attached to one paradigm that you can't see the next one coming.

And then there's the longer sweep of the history of science and technology. I find it very useful to think about how the Industrial Revolution unfolded, or how electricity took decades to actually transform factories after it was invented. It reminds me that the invention is only part of the story. The diffusion, the institutions, the way society adapts, all of that takes much longer, and it's where the real impact happens. So when I think about what AI will do to the world, I try to think on those timescales rather than on the timescale of the next conference deadline.

Finally, I'd say history makes you a bit more tolerant of your own failures. You read about Darwin sitting on his theory for twenty years, or about all the dead ends in physics, and you realize that this is just what research looks like. It's slow, it's messy, and the people who made the big contributions were usually the ones who kept going.

r001.rationale: The response uses electricity and computer vision history to inform current AI thinking, but does not say that historical situations are analogues whose details do not repeat exactly.

r002.rationale: It says research is slow and messy and that history helps tolerate failure, but does not connect the early immaturity of established sciences to confidence in persisting with AI research before results arrive.

r003.rationale: It says generations of AI researchers expected intelligence to be solved within a few years and were wrong about how long it would take, leading the speaker to hold current confident predictions loosely.

r004.rationale: The response notes that breakthroughs can come from unexpected directions, but does not state that people underestimate AI’s long-term progress because of discoveries they cannot currently anticipate.

astra-6.text:
History gives me a sense of perspective. When you are working in a field like AI, it is very easy to believe that whatever is exciting today is the culmination of everything that came before. Reading history reminds you that people in many periods have felt that way—and that progress is usually much less straightforward.

It also encourages me to look at ideas in their context. An idea may fail because it is wrong, but it may also fail because the tools, the data, or the computing resources are not yet available. So when we revisit an old problem, the useful question is: what has actually changed?

For me, that leads to a combination of optimism and humility. We can make substantial progress, but we should be careful about assuming that our current methods are the final answer.

r001.rationale: The response compares present excitement with attitudes in earlier periods, but does not clearly present those situations as useful analogues that do not exactly repeat the past.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss early-stage established sciences as grounds for persisting with AI research before results arrive.

r003.rationale: It cautions that progress is less straightforward than current excitement suggests, but does not state that people overestimate the pace of AI advances in the short term.

r004.rationale: It does not attribute underestimated long-term AI progress to discoveries that cannot currently be anticipated.

sol-6.1.text:
Reading history gives you a sense of perspective. When you’re living through a particular moment, it’s very easy to believe that whatever is exciting right now is the whole story. History reminds you that ideas have predecessors, that progress takes unexpected turns, and that people can be very confident and still be wrong.

That’s useful in AI because we have these waves of enthusiasm. I try to step back and ask: What is the underlying scientific problem? What have we actually understood, and what remains unexplained? You want to be enthusiastic enough to pursue a new idea, but skeptical enough to examine the evidence. For me, history encourages that combination of curiosity and humility.
